Document purpose

  • This guide provides configuration details for implementing VMware Cloud Foundation on Dell servers and PowerFlex storage. It demonstrates how to use the SDC as VMFS on FC as principal storage for both the management and the workload domain, removing the reliance on vSAN.

    Note: The contents of this document are valid for the software and hardware versions described. For information about updated configurations for newer software and hardware versions, contact your Red Hat or Dell Technologies sales representative.

    Note: Dell encountered numerous issues with the VCF Installer 9.0.1 during this implementation that required assistance from Broadcom to resolve. It is possible, therefore, to encounter issues during implementation that will require assistance from Broadcom support. Broadcom’s software issues are not related to the use of the Dell PowerFlex. An example of an issue is available in the Installation troubleshooting section of the Appendix.

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Using Dell PowerFlex with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 > Domains

Domains

  • A domain is part of a fleet and is comprised of the vCenter, NSX Manager, vSphere Cluster (hosts and storage), and SDDC Manager. There are two types of domains in VCF: management and workload. The management domain is the set of resources that runs VCF and is the control center of the environment, responsible for hosting the management plane VMs. There is one management domain per VCF instance, though there can be multiple per VCF fleet.

    Note: Prior to VCF 9, the SDDC Manager was the central management tool. While it is possible to continue to use SDDC Manager for some tasks, VCF Operations is the new recommended interface.

    You deploy workload domains from the VCF Operations inventory, and they consist of the same components as the management domains; however, they have no management VMs. They are part of the VCF instance. You typically use workload domains to run the applications for a business. You can have up to twenty-four workload domains in a VCF instance.

    In a typical configuration, you deploy separate nodes for the management and workload domains. For customers with fewer server resources or who want a smaller footprint or a POC lab, the management domain can also be a workload domain. This configuration is known as a consolidated architecture and can host customer workloads.

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Using Dell PowerFlex with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 > ESXi installation

ESXi installation

  • You must image each host used in the VCF deployment for the management domain with the correct release of 9.0 referenced in the BOM (build 24957456 for 9.0.1 GA release). Once installed complete these additional tasks.

    • Set the IP, network information, and hostname post-installation.
    • Log in to the vSphere Host Client and enable SSH. Regenerate the certificates so that they match the hostname. To regenerate the certificates, SSH to the host as root and run /sbin/generate-certificates. Then reboot the host. Technically, only hostd and vpxa require restart, but in testing that has not always been effective. A reboot guarantees success. The VCF installer will validate the hostname and certificate during deployment and if you do not regenerate beforehand, validation will fail.
    • Finally, set and start the NTP server on each ESXi host. You should use the same NTP server in use with the VCF installer This is an additional check the installer will do, though it will only produce a warning if it fails, at which point you can skip it.

    Note: In a greenfield deployment, the VCF installer requires the root password to be the same for all ESXi hosts for the management domain. A greenfield deployment only applies if you use a flat network. The workload domain does not have this requirement.

Heartbeat for vSphere HA

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Using Dell PowerFlex with VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 > Heartbeat for vSphere HA

Heartbeat for vSphere HA

  • VMware uses a heartbeat mechanism to check on the health of ESXi hosts in a vCenter cluster with vSphere HA enabled. There are two heartbeat mechanisms, network and datastore. In a cluster, one of the ESXi hosts is primary and the others are secondary. Each secondary hosts communicates with the primary over the network first, but should that fail, the hosts use shared datastores where there are reserved heartbeat blocks. VMware recommends at least two shared datastores for heartbeating. Since heartbeating uses reserved blocks, you can utilize any shared datastores. Since the initial deployment of VCF only has a single shared datastore, Dell recommends creating two additional, small datastores on the PowerFlex and presenting them to all VCF hosts for heartbeating. Follow the same process in the section Volume and VMFS datastore.

    Once available, enable vSphere HA on the new VCF cluster in vCenter and navigate to the Heartbeat Datastores tab in Cluster Settings in Figure 24. Use the radio button Use datastores from the specified list and complement automatically if needed and check the boxes next to the newly created datastores. Click OK to complete. Note that each domain should have its own heartbeat datastores.

    Figure 24.    Heartbeat datastores

    After enabling vSphere HA, enable vSphere DRS before proceeding.

    Cluster remediation settings

    You must make one final configuration change in vCenter after enabling vSphere HA and DRS. Navigate to Lifecycle Manager -> Settings -> Images and click EDIT in the right-hand corner in Figure 25.

    Figure 25.    Lifecycle manager cluster images

    In the pop-up window check the box next to Migrate powered off and suspended VMs to other hosts in the cluster, if a host must enter maintenance mode. During a greenfield implementation, the VCF installer sets this but in brownfield you do it manually as in Figure 26. Click SAVE. Setting this prevents the VCF installer from erroring during the validation step.

    Figure 26.    Cluster remediation settings

Independent architecture 

  • In an independent, or disaggregated, architecture some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps to minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture is ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads. 

    Disaggregation gives organizations the freedom to choose different LCM options that best align with their operational models. Not only can PowerFlex Manager manage the LCM of PowerFlex storage infrastructure, it can also manage LCM of PowerFlex compute nodes.  With this freedom, there is also the choice to manage compute estates that connect to PowerFlex with other tooling.

Installation troubleshooting

  • There are many known issues impacting the VCF installer that could cause a failure during deployment. During this brownfield deployment, the installer would fail consistently at 33% in Figure 93. The error message was “Failed to install VMCA Certificate on SDDC Manager.” Unfortunately there are many causes related to this message, mostly around DNS. In this case, however, the resolution was to reboot the vCenter appliance and then click RETRY AND PROCEED WITH DEPLOYMENT. The installation then succeeded. Broadcom did not recommend this, rather we discovered it through trial and error. Broadcom support was unable to pinpoint the cause. Dell recommends that if you do experience an unexpected error during the installation, you open an SR with Broadcom support.

    Figure 93.    VCF installer failure

Introduction

  • One of the benefits of using array-based storage for VCF is the ability to use the features of the PowerFlex, such as local replication for backup and recovery of the management and workload domain volumes. Local copies can serve multiple purposes, from cloning, to restores and backups.

    PowerFlex offers snapshot capability for block storage – SCSI or NVMe – through both the UI and CLI. The following section walks through creating a snapshot in PowerFlex Manager for the volume backing the management domain. In addition, we cover snapshot policies which enable automated backups.

    Block snapshot

    In PowerFlex Manager, log in and navigate to Block > Volumes. Using the check box, select the Management-Domain. From the Protect menu select Create Snapshot in Figure 87.

    Figure 87.    Select management domain volume for snapshot

    PowerFlex presents the following dialog in Figure 88. The Snapshot name defaults to %vol%-snap-%i% which is <volume_name>-snap-<index_number> and will result in a name of Management-Domain-snap-1. The field accepts thirty-two characters if you wish to change it. The index number is simply a way to ensure unique names when you use the default naming. In addition, the Use secure snapshot option, checked here, prohibits deletion of the snapshot until the defined expiration period has elapsed. Click Create.

    Figure 88.    Snapshot options for block storage

    Successful completion results in the message and the new snapshot in Figure 89.

    Figure 89.    Successful snapshot

    From the snapshot page of the volume in Figure 90, you can clone it or restore it.

    Figure 90.    Snapshot – restore and clone

    Snapshot policies

    In additional to individual snapshots, PowerFlex provides the ability to setup snapshot policies which consist of snapshot and retention rules that automate how often to take a snapshot of a block volume and how long to retain them. You can only assign one snapshot policy to a volume. To create a snapshot policy log in to PowerFlex Manager and take the following steps:

    1. Navigate to Protection -> Snapshot Policies
    2. Click Create Snapshot Policy
    3. Enter the following information in Figure 91.
      1. Policy Name.
      2. Snapshot Rules – specify by Minute, Hour, Day, or Week.
      3. Retention Rules – this defaults to a single rule based on the measure specified in the base rule, but two additional rules are possible, each modifying the length of the previous. In this example, the system creates a snapshot every six hours and then retains 7 days’ worth continuously. 
      4. Optionally you can secure the snapshots, however once you do you will be unable to modify the policy. You would have to create a new one.
    1. Click Create and Activate which allows you to assign the policy to a volume for immediate use. If you only Create, the policy enters a paused state. You can assign it to a volume but will be inoperable until activated.

    Figure 91.    Create snapshot policy

    Assign a volume to the policy by using the check box next to the policy and navigating to Protect -> Assign Volumes in Figure 92. Select the volume by checkbox and click Assign Policy.

    Figure 92.    Assign volumes

    The policy remains in effect for that volume unless you pause the policy or unassign the volume from it.

Lifecycle management

  • VCF has an integrated life cycle management function that facilitates the automation of upgrades to new versions. Because each version of VCF has a specific bill of materials, it is essential to use this function to maintain compliance. Figure 6 shows this interface in VCF Operations.

    Figure 6.   Lifecycle management

    PowerFlex

    Because VCF controls life cycle management, PowerFlex Manager cannot be used to manage the VCF software or SDC on the VCF nodes. It is possible, however, to add the VCF nodes in the Reserved Managed State as below.

    Figure 7.   PowerFlex Manager with VCF nodes in Reserved Managed State

    This permits updating the BIOS or firmware on the nodes. Be aware, however, that there is no integration between PowerFlex Manager and VCF. If you wish to update the BIOS or firmware you must manually put the VCF node into maintenance mode prior to updating any components and then remove maintenance mode after a presumed reboot of the node.

    Upgrades

    When upgrading, you start with the SDDC Manager. In Figure 6 an upgrade is in process to VCF 9.0.1. Once you upgrade the SDDC Manager to the chosen release, you can start with upgrading components of the management domain followed by the workload domains. It is not possible to run them concurrently. Note that when using the PowerFlex SDC, you need to follow a specific process outlined in the Appendix in VCF upgrades.

    Figure 8.   SDDC Manager upgrade

Network topology

  • For the environment in this paper the following networks exist. At the physical layer, there are two Top of Rack (TOR) switches used for redundancy and load-balancing purposes. There are two connections from each Dell host NIC used in the solution. We cabled one two-port NIC to TOR A and one two-port NIC to TOR B. VCF requires two NICs (minimum 10 GbE) to form a vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS).

    The following table shows the different configured VLANs in this solution. This environment is entirely private. Like this environment, most PowerFlex customers separate the data and management paths in a production configuration.

    Table 3.      Network VLANs

    Network type

    VLAN ID

    iDRAC management

    0

    Management, VM, vMotion, NSX and PowerFlex management

    16

    PowerFlex data

    1612, 1614

    In addition, we built a domain controller, DNS, and NTP server for the VCF deployment.

NVMe/TCP

  • NVMe/TCP is a storage protocol that allows you to access NVMe-based flash storage over standard TCP/IP networks, offering high performance without the need for specialized hardware like Fibre Channel or RDMA. When used with SAN storage like the PowerFlex, NVMe/TCP provides a scalable, low-latency alternative to traditional protocols like iSCSI, making it well-suited for all-flash environments and software-defined infrastructure. In VCF environments, NVMe/TCP enables ESXi hosts to connect to NVMe-capable PowerFlex arrays over standard 10/25/100 GbE networks, combining the performance advantages of NVMe with the simplicity and flexibility of IP networking. It integrates with VMware’s native multipathing and supports VMFS.

    NVMe/TCP PowerFlex

    PowerFlex hosts can use standard NVMe/TCP operating system drivers to connect to PowerFlex. They do not require proprietary host agents. VMware includes these drivers  in ESXi.

    Dell supports NVMe/TCP in a disaggregated, two-layer PowerFlex deployment architecture such as that deployed in this VCF solution. The NVMe host (ESXi) communicates directly with the NVMe target, which is known as the storage data target (SDT), on the storage node. Each storage node in this VCF PowerFlex 5.x installation contains an SDT seen in Figure 62. There is no additional setup on the PowerFlex other than adding the NVMe/TCP hosts (ESXi) in PowerFlex Manager after configuring NVMe/TCP on each workload domain ESXi host.

    Figure 62.    PowerFlex NVMe targets

    vSphere network

    If the NVMe/TCP storage network is physically separate from the other PowerFlex networks, you will need to create a new distributed switch in the workload domain vCenter. If the NVMe/TCP network uses the same VDS physical network on its own VLAN, create a new distributed port group. In this environment, although the NVMe/TCP storage network is the same as the SDC storage network, we need to create a new distributed port group for the same VLANs because NVMe/TCP does not support NIC teaming which is how we configured the existing distributed port group. We will create the distributed port groups and then modify the networking to adhere to VMware’s support.

    NVMe/TCP distributed port group

    To create a new distributed port group, you must log in directly to the vCenter. VCF Operations does not offer this capability.

    Step 1

    First, decide where you want to add supplemental storage – the management or workload domain. In this example we will use the workload domain. Log in to the workload domain vCenter as the administrator and navigate to the workload domain distributed network switch in the left-hand screen. In the right-hand screen click on ACTIONS -> Distributed Port Group -> New Distributed Port Group as below.

    Figure 63.    Step 1 – NVMe/TCP distributed port group

    Step 2

    Enter a new port group Name for NVMe/TCP. Dell recommends using a name that references the function. In this example in Figure 64 the name used is VLAN1612-TCP to distinguish it from the other port group with the same VLAN. Click NEXT.

    Figure 64.    Step 2 – NVMe/TCP distributed port group

    Step 3

    In the Configure settings below use the drop-down for VLAN type and select VLAN. Then enter a VLAN ID. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 65.    Step 3 – NVMe/TCP distributed port group

    Step 4

    Review the summary page and if correct, click FINISH.

    Figure 66.    Step 4 – NVMe/TCP distributed port group

    Load balancing and failover

    The NVMe over TCP adapter does not support such NIC teaming features as failover and load balancing. Instead, it relies on storage multipathing for these functions. Because both NICs are active in the VCF VDS configuration, it is necessary to set one of the active uplinks to unused in the distributed port group.

    Before editing the distributed port group, determine the association of physical NIC to uplink. This is critical because when you add the NVMe/TCP adapter to vSphere you must specify a physical NIC, and you must select the one with the active uplink and not the unused uplink.

    Uplink NIC association

    In vCenter, navigate to one of the ESXi hosts in the left-hand screen, then on the right-hand screen select Configure -> Networking -> Virtual switches. View the NSX VDS and on the right-hand side expand Uplink 1 and Uplink 2 to see the physical adapters, vmnic6 and vmnic7 respectively. Make note of this information.

    Figure 67.    Uplinks and associated NICs

    Modify distributed port group

    In vCenter highlight the NVMe/TCP distributed port group in the left-hand screen. In the right-hand screen navigate to ACTIONS -> Edit Settings….

    Figure 68.    Edit settings in distributed port group

    Select Teaming and failover in the left-hand menu in Figure 69. All uplinks will display under Active uplinks under Failover order in the right-hand screen. Highlight all uplinks but Uplink 1 and use the MOVE DOWN button to list them under the Unused uplinks. Recall that Uplink 1 is associated with vmnic6. Uplink 3 and Uplink 4 are idle, but it is best to move them also in case there is a new NIC association in the future. Click OK to complete.

    Figure 69.    Modify uplinks in distributed port group

    VMkernel adapters

    After creating and modifying the distributed port group, add a VMkernel adapter for each ESXi host.

    Step 1

    In Figure 70 navigate to the new distributed port group in the left-hand screen and in the right-hand screen select ACTIONS -> Add VMkernel Adapters…

    Figure 70.    Step 1 – Add VMkernel adapters

    Step 2

    Use the checkboxes to select all ESXi hosts in the workload domain. Click NEXT.

    Figure 71.    Step 2 – Add VMkernel adapters

    Step 3

    Select the Enabled services for the adapter which is NVMe over TCP. If you fail to check this box, it will not be possible to add the storage controllers in vSphere for NVMe/TCP even though the VMkernel adapters are there. Note you can check the box after creation if you forget. Click NEXT.

    Figure 72.    Step 3 – Add VMkernel adapters

    Step 4

    Next, either use DHCP or assign a static IP to each ESXi host. If you use static, once you enter the first IP, vSphere will offer to auto-fill the other IPs and subnets. The gateway is optional. Once complete click NEXT.

    Figure 73.    Step 4 – Add VMkernel adapters

    Step 5

    Finally, review the proposed changes and if acceptable click FINISH.

    Figure 74.    Step 5 – Add VMkernel adapters

    After vSphere adds the VMkernel adapters, it is a best practice to SSH into each ESXi host as root and run a vmkping to the IP interfaces on the array to ensure connectivity. Note that you may have to enable SSH first. There is an example below where we pinged both the new VMkernel IPs as well as one of the SDTs on the PowerFlex array.

    [root@vcf250:~] vmkping 172.18.100.150

    PING 172.18.100.150 (172.18.100.150): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.18.100.150: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.043 ms

    --- 172.18.100.150 ping statistics ---

    1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.043/0.043/0.043 ms

    [root@vcf250:~] vmkping 172.19.100.150

    PING 172.19.100.150 (172.19.100.150): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.19.100.150: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.046 ms

    --- 172.19.100.150 ping statistics ---

    1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.046/0.046/0.046 ms

    [root@vcf250:~] vmkping 172.18.100.230

    PING 172.18.100.230 (172.18.100.230): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.18.100.230: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.111 ms

    --- 172.18.100.230 ping statistics ---

    1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.111/0.111/0.111 ms

    [root@vcf250:~] vmkping 172.19.100.230

    PING 172.19.100.230 (172.19.100.230): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.19.100.230: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.113 ms

    --- 172.19.100.230 ping statistics ---

    1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.113/0.113/0.113 ms

    NVMe/TCP adapter

    For each ESXi host add an NVMe/TCP adapter. Do this in vCenter by highlighting an ESXi host in the left-hand screen and navigating to Configure -> Storage -> Storage Adapters in the right-hand screen. Use the drop-down list under ADD SOFTWARE ADAPTER to select Add NVMe over TCP Adapter. Use the drop-down in Figure 75 to select the NIC that is associated with Uplink 1 you set in Modify distributed port group.

    Figure 75.    Adding an NVMe/TCP adapter

    Repeat these steps for the other workload domain ESXi hosts.

    Storage controller

    It is now possible to add the PowerFlex array controllers to each ESXi host in the workload domain. You can add the controllers through either the vSphere UI or ESXi CLI. For PowerFlex, the CLI is more consistently successful than the UI and therefore we will use it here. We will start with the UI where it is important to check that the host NQN is set.

    Step 1

    In vCenter highlight an ESXi host in the left-hand screen and navigate to Configure -> Storage -> Storage Adapters in the right-hand screen. Scroll down the adapters to the bottom and use the radio button next to the newly added NVMe/TCP adapter. In the bottom panel select the Controllers tab and then click on ADD CONTROLLER in Figure 76.

    Figure 76.    Step 1 – Add controller

    Step 2

    In the Add controller screen check that the Host NQN is set. In the unlikely event it is not set, you will either need to restart the management agents or reboot ESXi. Do not proceed with the next step until it the field displays. Hit CANCEL to close the screen.

    Figure 77.    Step 2 – Add controller

    Step 3

    Log in to the ESXi host as root. For each SDT node run the following command to add the controllers. Provide the correct vmhba and IP address.

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhbaxx -i <SDT IP> -p 8009 -c

    As noted, this PowerFlex system possess five SDT nodes, each with two IP addresses, resulting in the following ten commands:

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.18.100.230 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.19.100.230 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.18.100.231 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.19.100.231 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.18.100.232 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.19.100.232 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.18.100.233 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.19.100.233 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.18.100.234 -p 8009 -c

    esxcli nvme fabrics discover -a vmhba65 -i 172.19.100.234 -p 8009 -c

    To view the connected controllers, execute the following command in Figure 78.

    Figure 78.    Step 3 – Add controller

    Step 4

    You can now return to the UI to see the controllers. Highlight the adapter and run RESCAN ADAPTER and the newly added controllers will show up.

    Figure 79.    Step 4 – Add controller

    Storage provisioning

    With connectivity established, you can provision storage. First, add the new NVMe hosts and then create and map a volume.

    Hosts

    Start by obtaining the host NQNs for each workload ESXi domain host in the Add controller screen. Log in to PowerFlex Manager and navigate to Block -> Hosts. Click Add Host and fill in a chosen Host Name and supply the Host NQN in Figure 80. Click Add to complete. Repeat for other hosts.

    Figure 80.    Add NVMe host

    Volume provisioning

    As we covered provisioning in Volume and VMFS datastore, it is unnecessary to repeat all steps. The volume detail is in Figure 81. We are using a 2 TB volume.

    Figure 81.    Supplemental volume

    Map the volume to the new NVMe hosts.

    Figure 82.    Map supplemental volume

    View the new device in vCenter. NVMe/TCP adapters rarely require rescans for the storage to be visible.

    Figure 83.    NVMe/TCP devices in vCenter

    Datastores

    Creating a datastore on a NVMe/TCP device does not differ in any way from those created on SCSI-based devices. Using the datastore wizard in Figure 84, the NVMe/TCP devices are available for use.

    Figure 84.    Using NVMe/TCP device for supplemental storage datastore

    Complete the wizard and the NVMe/TCP datastore will display in vCenter in Figure 85 and in VCF Operations in Figure 86, alongside the workload domain FC datastore for the cluster.

    Figure 85.    vCenter view of supplemental storage

    Figure 86.    VCF Operations view of supplemental storage

    The supplemental storage is now available for workload domain applications designated for NVMe/TCP.

Overview

  • VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, or VCF, is a complete software-defined infrastructure platform that encompasses all the required components to run a private, public, or hybrid cloud. VCF 9.0 focuses specifically on the private cloud experience using VCF Operations as the central control hub. From VCF Operations, the user can control all aspects of the VCF environment, from day-to-day troubleshooting to new workload deployments. The other components of the VCF platform include vSphere for compute, vSAN for storage, NSX for networking, SDDC Manager, and VCF Automation.

    VCF uses the concept of domains. There are two domains: management and workload. The management domain is the heart of the VCF implementation and requires NFS, VMFS on FC, or vSAN storage to deploy. It is responsible for hosting the many management plane VMs, but it can also host customer VMs when employing a consolidated architecture without a separate workload domain. VMware designed a workload domain to run customer workloads. A single vCenter Server instance manages a workload domain and can consist of one or more vSphere clusters. In VCF 9.0, you can deploy the workload domain on all the same storage options as the management domain. The flexibility in storage options in VCF 9.0 permits the use of more robust storage array solutions like the PowerFlex without the need for vSAN in the solution.

    This paper provides an overview of how to implement a VCF 9.0 environment on a PowerFlex platform using VMFS on FC for principal storage via the SDC. It covers deployment of both the management and workload domains, including PowerFlex storage provisioning.

PowerFlex consumption options 

  • PowerFlex rack 

    PowerFlex rack is a software-defined infrastructure platform that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified network. This rack-based engineered system, with integrated networking, enables customers to achieve the scalability and management requirements of a modern data center.  

    PowerFlex appliance 

    PowerFlex appliance is a PowerEdge-based server which has been configured to be a node in a software-defined storage deployment that runs PowerFlex software components. This offering allows customers the flexibility and savings to bring their own compatible networking or make use of full network automation using a supported set of Dell or Cisco switches. 

    PowerFlex custom nodes 

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes are validated PowerEdge-based server building-blocks configured for use with PowerFlex. They are available with thousands of configuration options for customers who prefer to build their own environments.

    PowerFlex in the public cloud 

    PowerFlex software storage services can be deployed on recommended instances (with attached storage) in Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure. Only the EC and MG data layout as well as the Independent (disaggregated) architecture are supported. Where available, native asynchronous replication may be used to migrate data between cloud and on-premises PowerFlex systems, or to establish cloud-based BC/DR data protection schemes.

PowerFlex CSI/CSM  

  • An important component outside of PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After loading the CSI driver for PowerFlex into Kubernetes, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance. 

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod.  

    Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules: 

    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications. 
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations. 
    • Extends storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include replication, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency.  

    PowerFlex supports multiple operating systems. PowerFlex is validated with the leading Kubernetes distributions as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 2.   PowerFlex for different Kubernetes distributions

PowerFlex topology

  • The PowerFlex 5.0 system in this solution consists of five nodes, three for the MDM cluster and two for Tie Breakers. This meets the minimum requirement for a 2 + 2 protection scheme. You could also use a minimum of eleven nodes for an 8 + 2 protection scheme. Refer to the PowerFlex documentation for more details. The characteristics of the servers in this solution are as follows:

Prerequisites

  • You must meet the following minimum prerequisites before implementing VCF on PowerFlex using VMFS on FC as principal storage via the SDC. We cover storage provisioning in a later section.

    • Server requirements for VCF management and workload domains are as follows:
    • A minimum of four Dell servers with sufficient networking, memory, CPU, and local storage to satisfy the requirements of the VCF management domain.
    • A minimum of two Dell servers with sufficient networking, memory, CPU, and local storage to satisfy the requirements of a VCF workload domain running on VMFS on FC.
    • Storage requirements for VCF management and workload domains are as follows:
    • Implementation of PowerFlex Manager (PFMP).
    • The PowerFlex system must be two-layer. You cannot implement VCF on an HCI configuration. This implementation uses storage from a PowerFlex 5.0 implementation which does not support HCI.
    • You must obtain licenses for the VCF solution. A default evaluation license is in place for 90 days.

SDC installation

  • Each of the ESXi hosts in the management domain also serve as PowerFlex compute-only nodes. Because VCF dictates the ESXi version, you cannot use the template process in PowerFlex Manager to deploy the compute-only nodes. Therefore, after installation of ESXi and the vCenter, you must install the SDC component manually on each host. The installation requires three reboots of the host.

    The following section details a manual installation of the SDC and daemon agent and the provisioning and mapping of a volume for creation of a VMFS datastore for the management domain.

    Manual SDC installation

    Locate the released version of the SDC and daemon agent for ESXi 9 and the 5.x PowerFlex release in use. Copy these zip files to a local datastore on each ESXi host. Then perform the following steps as root:

    1. Set the acceptance level for the .zip install: esxcli software acceptance set --level PartnerSupported

    [root@vcf241:~] esxcli software acceptance set --level PartnerSupported

    Host acceptance level changed to 'PartnerSupported'.

    1. Install the SDC zip: esxcli software component apply -d /vmfs/volumes/local_241/sdc-5.1.0.293-esx9.x.zip

    [root@vcf241:~] esxcli software component apply -d  /vmfs/volumes/local_241/sdc-5.1.0.293-esx9.x.zip

    Installation Result

       Message: The update completed successfully, but the system needs to be rebooted for the changes to be effective.

       Components Installed: scaleio-sdc-esx9x_5.1.0.293-1OEM.900.0.24755229

       Components Removed:

       Components Skipped:

       Reboot Required: true

       DPU Results:

    1. Install the agent daemon zip: esxcli software component apply -d  /vmfs/volumes/local_241/sdc-agent-5.1.0.234-esx9.x.zip

    [root@vcf241:~] esxcli software component apply -d  /vmfs/volumes/local_241/sdc-agent-5.1.0.234-esx9.x.zip

    Installation Result

       Message: The update completed successfully, but the system needs to be rebooted for the changes to be effective.

       Components Installed: scaleio-daemon-esx_5.1.0.234-0

       Components Removed:

       Components Skipped:

       Reboot Required: true

       DPU Results:

    1. Reboot the host.
    2. Generate a unique GUID: GUID generation
    3. Set the MDM IPs (actual or virtual) and GUID for the ESXi host: esxcli system module parameters set -m scini -p "IoctlIniGuidStr=<GUID> IoctlMdmIPStr=<comma separated MDM IPs>"

    [root@vcf241:~] esxcli system module parameters set -m scini -p "IoctlIniGuidStr=40b7f5f7-1f42-4c2f-9cb4-77a6ad56086d IoctlMdmIPStr=172.16.50.229,172.16.50.230,172.16.50.231"

    1. Reboot the host.

    When the host comes back up, it should appear in the Block -> Hosts list in PowerFlex Manager. All four management domain hosts appear below post-installation.

    Figure 12.    SDC hosts

    SDC in VMware

    To view how VMware represents the SDC, log in to an ESXI host as in Figure 13 and navigate in the left-menu pane to Storage and then the Adapters tab on the right panel. Locate the vmhba adapter that lists the Driver as scini, in this example it is vmhba64. Note the Model is empty. The SDC creates this faux HBA adapter in order to present IP-based PowerFlex storage. This adapter is what permits the use of PowerFlex storage as VMFS on FC since VMware assumes this is FC-attached storage. Note that in the vCenter in Figure 14, the Type is Fibre Channel. 

    Figure 13.    SDC representation in ESXi

    Figure 14.    SDC representation in vCenter

    Volume and VMFS datastore

    After you install the SDC on each host, create a volume through PowerFlex Manager and map that volume to each of the hosts. This volume will serve as the VMFS datastore for the management domain deployment.

    Step 1

    Begin by navigating in PowerFlex Manager to Block -> Volumes. Click Create Volume in the left-hand corner, enter in the required information, and click Create in Figure 15. Dell recommends a minimum of 4 TB for the volume/datastore, though here we used 8 TB.

    Figure 15.    Step 1 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 2

    When the grey pop-up box appears after volume creation in Figure 15, click Map. If the box disappears too quickly, simply check the box next to the new volume and navigate to Provision -> Map. In the mapping screen below, use the check boxes to select each new ESXi management node and click Map.

    Figure 16.    Step 2 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 3

    You must create a new VMFS datastore on the volume after you map it to the hosts. Log in to the vCenter, right-click on the cluster and select Storage -> New Datastore to start the datastore wizard.

    Figure 17.    Step 3 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 4

    Begin by selecting the datastore type. In this deployment we use VMFS. Click NEXT.

    Figure 18.    Step 4 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 5

    Enter a Datastore name that identifies its purpose. In this implementation the name is MGMT_DOMAIN. Next select one of the ESXi hosts from the drop-down list. As we mapped the volume to all the hosts, any one will work. You will see a list of available volumes, among which will be the 8 TB (in this example) PowerFlex volume. Use the radio button to highlight it and click NEXT.

    Figure 19.    Step 5 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 6

    When you choose VMFS as the type you must choose with which version to format the volume. Dell recommends using the default VMFS 6. Click NEXT after choosing.

    Figure 20.    Step 6 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 7

    In the Partition configuration screen do not change the defaults and click NEXT to review.

    Figure 21.    Step 7 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 8

    In the last step, review and then click FINISH to create the datastore.

    Figure 22.    Step 8 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Once the datastore appears in the list of available datastores in Figure 23, be sure that each ESXi recognizes the new datastore before proceeding. This may require running a Rescan Storage… seen in Figure 17.

    Figure 23.    MGMT_DOMAIN datastore

    Note: After creating the datastore for the management domain, Dell strongly recommends using Storage vMotion to relocate the vCenter VM to the new datastore. There is a known Broadcom issue in which the VMs the installer creates will deploy to the datastore where the vCenter resides, even if it is local. If the datastore is small, the installer will fail.

Storage

  • In VCF there are two distinct categories of storage, each serving a separate function in the solution. These categories are: principal and supplemental. You employ principal storage to deploy a management or workload domain or to deploy a new cluster into an existing workload. Supplemental storage, on the other hand, is storage you add to any existing management or workload domain post-deployment. For new installations (greenfield), Broadcom restricts principal storage to four types: vSAN, VMFS on FC, vVols, or NFS v3. The management domain only supports vSAN, VMFS on FC, or NFS v3; but you can utilize the fourth type, vVols, for workload domains, with Broadcom’s permission. Supplemental storage supports all principal storage types as well as iSCSI, NVMe/TCP, and NFS v4.1. Note that due to the unique way that the PowerFlex SDC presents devices through a virtual FC adapter, its storage falls under the VMFS on FC category. The following image represents the differences between the storage types.

     

    Figure 5.   VCF 9.0 storage options

    It is important to understand that vSAN is the only storage VCF can completely control as part of the lifecycle of an instance. If you present storage using another protocol from an array like Dell PowerFlex, the administrator has the responsibility of managing it. For example, if you need to expand a datastore on the PowerFlex, you will use PowerFlex Manager to expand the device and then manually expand the datastore in vCenter or the vSphere Client.

Summary

  • VMware Cloud Foundation provides a complete, unified platform to build both a private and public cloud, combining compute, storage, networking, and management. VCF offers the flexibility of using various storage options to take advantage of the power and scalability of external arrays like PowerFlex.

    VCF supports VMFS on FC using the PowerFlex SDC for both the management and workload domains, removing the need for vSAN. The PowerFlex provides both superior performance and advanced features like local replication for backup and recovery. When using PowerFlex it enables the VCF environment to become highly resilient, scalable, and able to handle the most demanding workload domains.

    By following the guidelines outlined in this paper, the user can ensure the successful implementation of VCF 9 running on a PowerFlex.

vCenter installation

  • After imaging the ESXi hosts, deploy a new vCenter for the management domain. A pre-configured vCenter is the only way to satisfy the network requirements of a PowerFlex implementation where there are separate physical management and data networks.

    Note: If the PowerFlex shares a single physical network (i.e., flat) for management and data, you can utilize a VCF greenfield deployment which does not require a manually installed vCenter.

    Download the vCenter ISO build recorded in Table 2 and mount on an appropriate jump host with access to the ESXi hosts. You must install the new vCenter on one of the newly imaged ESXi hosts. Though not best practice, the VCF installer requires this configuration, or the deployment will fail a check and will not proceed. In addition, be sure to follow VCF password guidelines for the vCenter. If your password does not meet the minimum requirements that VCF sets, you will be unable to ingest it during deployment and will have to modify it post-installation.

    Once the vCenter is up, create a new datacenter and cluster in it. The naming is completely arbitrary. Add the ESXi hosts to the new cluster. Do not enable DRS or HA on the cluster as you will do this after the creation of datastores. Figure 9 is the vCenter used in this implementation.

    Figure 9.   vCenter deployment

    Virtual Distributed Switches (VDS)

    After the initial vCenter configuration, you need to create the virtual distributed switches, or VDS, which permit access to the PowerFlex management and data networks. Each network should have a VMkernel adapter. While the data networks do not require any services, you should enable vMotion for the management network. Dell recommends at least four 10 GbE NICs for such a configuration which will offer redundancy for each of the two VDS.

    Create each VDS, adding two physical NICs to each switch. PowerFlex recommends disabling Network I/O Control as a best practice. This environment has the following two VDS.

    Figure 10.    Distributed switches

    Add distributed port groups as required to each VDS. There are three in this setup, VLAN16 for the management network on pfvcf-cl01-vds01 and VLAN1612 and VLAN1614 for the data networks on pfvcf-cl01-vds02.

    Figure 11.    Distributed port groups

    Test

    When you complete the network configuration, log in to each ESXi host as root and execute vmkping to each PowerFlex management and data IP address. This will ensure that when you install the SDC it will be able to communicate with the PowerFlex storage and permit you to map volumes to the ESXi hosts.

    [root@vcf241:~] vmkping 172.16.100.230

    PING 172.16.100.230 (172.16.100.230): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.16.100.230: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.102 ms

    64 bytes from 172.16.100.230: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.105 ms

    64 bytes from 172.16.100.230: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.090 ms

    --- 172.16.100.230 ping statistics ---

    3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.090/0.099/0.105 ms

    [root@vcf241:~] vmkping 172.18.100.230

    PING 172.18.100.230 (172.18.100.230): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.18.100.230: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.103 ms

    64 bytes from 172.18.100.230: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.085 ms

    64 bytes from 172.18.100.230: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.113 ms

    --- 172.18.100.230 ping statistics ---

    3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss

    round-trip min/avg/max = 0.085/0.100/0.113 ms

    [root@vcf241:~] vmkping 172.19.100.230

    PING 172.19.100.230 (172.19.100.230): 56 data bytes

    64 bytes from 172.19.100.230: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.119 ms

    64 bytes from 172.19.100.230: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.101 ms

    64 bytes from 172.19.100.230: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.104 ms

    [root@vcf241:~]

    Cleanup

    During the creation of the VDS you will migrate the management network from the default vSwitch. This will leave an empty vSwitch on each ESXi host. Be sure to remove it. Additionally, if there is a BMC vSwitch, remove it and the VMkernel adapter for it. If these remain they will cause errors during the VCF deployment. The distributed switches should be the only host switches in the vCenter prior to the VCF installation.

VCF installation

  • Although VCF consists of multiple software releases you do not have to install the components independently. To install the management domain use the VMware Cloud Foundation Installer which includes all the necessary software.

    Deployment types

    There are two distinct types of VCF deployments, greenfield and brownfield (also known as “converged”). While a greenfield deployment requires the software versions detailed in Table 2, a brownfield deployment has greater flexibility both in software and storage to facilitate the consumption of existing infrastructure. Because of the greenfield network limitations in the VCF installer, a PowerFlex implementation which physically separates management from data networks requires brownfield. Despite being brownfield, the deployment documented in this paper is a new VCF implementation for both the management and workload domains. Therefore it uses the software versions in Table 2 and follows the rules for principal storage. If you are converting an existing vSphere setup to VCF 9.0, refer to VMware’s VCF documentation in the References.

    Greenfield deployment

    There are three steps to installation in a greenfield deployment.

    1. Prepare the environment. You can prepare your installation through the Planning and Preparation Workbook that VMware provides. The worksheet is optional but helps guide the user on all the necessary information to complete the deployment wizard.
    2. Image all servers with the correct ESXi version from the Bill of Materials. This installation is straightforward, choosing among the available methods, and then you make minor post-installation modifications. ESXi is the only software that the VMware Cloud Foundation Installer does not install when doing a greenfield deployment.
    3. Install VMware Cloud Foundation and download or upload the BOM software releases. This installation requires first deploying the VMware Cloud Foundation Installer appliance which is a wizard-driven application used to create the management domain.

    Brownfield deployment

    A VCF greenfield deployment requires a single physical network, employing different VLANs for some components if desired. Most PowerFlex deployments, however, separate the data and management networks physically, not simply by VLAN. Prior to VCF 9, it was not possible to use two physical networks and separate the data and management paths. In VCF 9 it is now possible to do this, however you must use a brownfield deployment, not greenfield. Therefore, in addition to imaging all the servers with ESXi, you must also deploy a vCenter of the appropriate version in the BOM and complete additional steps.

    Note: The brownfield deployment described here is specific to a new PowerFlex VCF 9.0 implementation. It is not meant to cover all the ways a customer can “converge” an existing VMware infrastructure into VCF. The purpose is to mimic a greenfield deployment as closely as possible which requires that you manually install only one single component, the vCenter.

    The brownfield deployment steps are:

    1. Prepare the environment. You can prepare your installation through the Planning and Preparation Workbook that VMware provides. The worksheet is optional but helps guide the user on all the necessary information to complete the deployment wizard.
    1. Image all servers with the correct ESXi version from the Bill of Materials. This installation is straightforward, choosing among the available methods, and then you make minor post-installation modifications.
    2. Install a vCenter on one of the newly imaged ESXi hosts. Though not best practice, you must deploy the vCenter on one of the VCF hosts or the installation will error.
      1. Add all the imaged hosts to the new vCenter in a new datacenter and cluster. Do not enable DRS or HA initially on the cluster.
      2. Create the new virtual distributed switches (VDS) for the management and data networks. Add the ESXi host to the VDS.
      3. Install the SDC agent and driver software on each ESXi host and configure the parameters for the GUID, MDM IP(s), and kernel. Be sure that each ESXi host can ping the management and data networks prior to setting the parameters.
      4. Create two small devices on the PowerFlex and present them to the ESXi hosts. Then create two datastores on them. These shared datastores are necessary for HA heart beating.
      5. Enable DRS and HA on the vSphere cluster.
    3. Install VMware Cloud Foundation and download or upload the BOM software releases. This installation requires first deploying the VMware Cloud Foundation Installer appliance which is a wizard-driven application used to create the management domain.

    The next section covers the installation of the management domain using a brownfield deployment, including the prerequisites.

VCF Operations

  • VCF Operations is the heart of VCF 9.0, taking the place of SDDC Manager as the primary management tool. The UI login is in Figure 41.

    Figure 41.    VCF Operations login

    Once accessed, you can see the various screens and sub-screens in the left-hand menu in Figure 42. Note that vSAN Cluster displays Not Configured for an array deployment such as this one.

    Figure 42.    VCF health for the instance

VCF upgrades

  • When the VCF domains are comprised of servers that are also compute-only nodes of a two-layer PowerFlex deployment, as in this paper, VCF must still control lifecycle management. This is because of the strict requirements of the BOM, and in particular the ESXi version. If you allow PowerFlex to upgrade ESXi outside of VCF, it will render the environment unsupported. Therefore, you must upgrade components like the SDC manually.

    VCF will recognize the SDC as a third-party VIB in the Lifecycle screen of VCF Operations in Figure 94. For minor ESXi updates that do not change the base version, e.g., 9.x, the SDC will not require an update. If VCF releases a new ESXi major release in conjunction with VCF, for example VCF 10 with ESXi 10, you will have to manually upgrade the SDC. The upgrade is a remove and replace operation – remove the SDC prior to the lifecycle upgrade and then install the updated version post-upgrade. Dell recommends working with your Broadcom representative to plan the upgrade steps.

    Figure 94.    Third-Party Custom VIBs Details for the SDC

VMware Cloud Foundation

  • VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) is a complete software-defined management solution that consists of VMware vSphere, VMware NSX Manager, VMware vSAN, and VCF Automation and Operations. VMware Cloud Foundation Installer drives the installation of VCF. The various components serve the following roles:

    • VMware Cloud Foundation Installer: A virtual appliance that the user deploys that automates the building of the management domain of VCF. You provision subsequent domains through VCF Operations.
    • SDDC Manager: Automates the life cycle management of VCF. It enables updating and upgrades, firmware application, and the general day-to-day operation of VCF.
    • VMware vSphere: Virtualizes the bare-metal servers using the ESXi software and aggregates them in the vCenter Server.
    • VMware NSX Manager: Provides the networking for the VCF solution along with security and automation. The design of NSX is for both private and public clouds.
    • VMware vSAN: An optional component that aggregates local or direct-attached storage in a single shared pool across all ESXi hosts in the VCF environment.
    • VMware Cloud Foundation Automation: Empowers IT to deliver self-service cloud experience for AI, Kubernetes, and VM-based applications. It provides a platform for deploying and managing applications and services, enabling end-users to consume and manage resources in a self-service fashion.
    • VMware Cloud Foundation Operations: Provides a unified interface and set of capabilities to help organizations build, operate, and secure their cloud infrastructures built on VCF.

    VMware portrays the high-level VCF implementation as depicted below.

    Figure 3.   VMware Cloud Foundation

VMware Cloud Foundation Installer

  • The VMware Cloud Foundation Installer is a virtual appliance with a UI that guides the user through a VCF installation. Prior to this release, the installer (aka Cloud Builder) relied on the use of an Excel spreadsheet. The spreadsheet itself still exists for the purpose of planning the installation. It is the vcf-9.0-planning-and-preparation-workbook.xls and is at located at VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook. It is useful for recording all the information necessary to complete the wizard, though optional.

    Note: While the VMware Cloud Foundation Installer is the preferred method for a VCF installation, there is a VCF CLI. The major difference between the UI and CLI is the ability to highly customize a CLI installation. Environments with unique networking requirements, for example, may require the use of the CLI, though the UI does permit changes to the standard network setup.

    Deploy the appliance on an existing ESXi host or vCenter with access to the networking of the VCF environment. Once deployed, log in as the admin@local user. The screen in Figure 27 appears. Unlike the previous VCF installer, this one requires the user to either download (online depot) or upload (offline) the software products for the chosen deployment type. Note that the Download Binaries panel will always list the initial release 9.0.0, though in this example the binaries for 9.0.1 are available.

    Figure 27.    VMware Cloud Foundation Installer

    Click on the DEPOT SETTINGS button in the Download Binaries box to configure the depot and download the components for the chosen install. Figure 28 shows we pulled the 9.0.1 VCF binaries from the depot. We did not download the vCenter because as this is a brownfield implementation the installer will not deploy the vCenter, rather we did so previously as a prerequisite. The Download Status of each component will show either a green circle with Success or a blue circle with Not downloaded. Note that Broadcom lists new versions or patches of VCF under Binary Management as below for 9.0.1.0.

    Figure 28.    Binary Management

    Once you successfully download all components, the deployment can begin. In the Deploy box on the right in Figure 21, use the drop-down menu of the DEPLOYMENT WIZARD and select VMware Cloud Foundation which we boxed in green.

    Prior to starting the installation, you must select whether this is a new VCF Fleet or an installation into an existing VCF implementation. Figure 29 presents the two options. Use the radio buttons to choose the appropriate installation. Though this paper documents a brownfield installation, it still represents a new VCF Fleet. Click CONTINUE to start the wizard in earnest.

    Note: Before starting the deployment, Dell strongly recommends that you take a VMware crash-consistent snapshot of the VCF installer and vCenter. This will allow you to re-deploy cleanly should the need arise.

    Figure 29.    VCF fleet deployment options

    The VCF wizard consists of steps which vary in number based on selections you make during implementation. The steps follow the order of the boxes in Figure 29, beginning with VCF Operations. Helpfully, the installer will save your steps as you proceed so you can leave the process at any point and return where you left off. This section will walk through those steps. We include the images as it is likely future releases of the installer will change.

    Step 1 Existing Components

    Even if you select to deploy a new VCF fleet, you can choose to incorporate existing software, specifically VCF Operations or VMware vCenter as we do in this example. When you select VMware vCenter you can also indicate to the installer whether NSX Manager is already part of the setup. It is not here, so this remains unchecked. Note that in Figure 24 when we select VMware vCenter, on the right-hand side an “Existing” blue box appears for vCenter and vSphere Cluster. This also reduces the number of steps to nine. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 30.    Step 1 – Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 2 General Information

    In step 2 the version defaults to 9.0.1.0. Supply the VCF instance and management domain names. Choose whether you wish VCF Operations and Automation to use a different network than the rest of the install. If you plan on multiple VCF instances in your fleet, you may wish to do that. Next, select a deployment model. Unless this is a test environment, you should use the HA option. Depending on the selected deployment model, the screens for steps 3, 4, and 6 will appear differently. The HA option requires more host (FQDN) names since there are three nodes, not one, for VCF Operations, VCF Automation, and NSX Manager. Click NEXT.

    Figure 31.    Step 2 – Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 3 VCF Operations

    There are four sections requiring information in step 3: VCF Operations Appliance, Load Balancer (optional), Fleet Management Appliance, and Operations Collector Appliance. Use the checkbox in each section if desired, as here, to set an appliance to the same password as VCF Operations. Click NEXT.

    Figure 32.    Step 3 – Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 4 VCF Automation

    In step 1 you had the option to choose to use an existing VCF Operations instance. Similarly, in step 4 you can bypass installing VCF Automation and connect one later; otherwise, supply the necessary FQDN and IPs. Note that in the image on the right, a white checkmark in a green circle appears for each step as you move through the wizard. Click NEXT.

    Figure 33.    Step 4 – Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 5 vCenter

    For the existing vCenter supply the FQDN, the root password, the SSO domain name, and the SSO password. A prompt will appear allowing you to confirm the Certificate Thumbprint. Because we already configured a datastore and the network in the vCenter, there are no additional steps in the installer for those components. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 34.    Step 5 - Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 6 NSX Manager

    The NSX Manager requires an appliance size and four FQDNs. In the second half of the screen, VCF offers the ability to create an NSX Overlay without the need for a separate VLAN. Dell recommends using this option. Input all necessary passwords and click NEXT.

    Figure 35.    Step 6 – Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 7 SDDC Manager

    For the SDDC Manager step provide an FQDN and the requested passwords. Click NEXT.

    Figure 36.    Step 7 - Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 8 Review

    In step 12 in Figure 37 review your answers. If anything is incorrect, you can go back and change it in that step and return to this screen. You will not have to travel all the steps again. If you wish, download the JSON spec. This is highly recommended because if you must re-install or start over you can supply the JSON and then edit in the wizard without inputting again. When ready hit NEXT.

    Figure 37.    Step 8 - Deploy VCF Fleet

    Step 9 Validate & Deploy

    The final screen runs an automatic validation of the previous input values. You can acknowledge any warnings but must resolve any errors. Network errors are common such as an inability to reach the DNS or a gateway, though less so in a brownfield implementation where these components must already be operational. You can bypass any warning by acknowledging it after verifying. Here all checks pass so click DEPLOY.

    Figure 38.    Step 9 - Deploy VCF Fleet

    Once you click DEPLOY VMware will present the progress screen in Figure 39 where you can actively watch the installation and the current task.

    Figure 39.    VCF installation progress screen

    The deployment time varies according to the environment but can take hours. You must resolve any errors during the installation and attempt the deployment again. There is no cleanup or reset, though if you took snapshots of the VCF installer and vCenter you could restore them to start fresh with the JSON file. Troubleshooting information is available from Broadcom here.

    When the deployment succeeds, the installer presents the screen in Figure 40. Click the OPEN VCF OPERATIONS UI button in the right-hand panel to log in to VCF Operations and add your licensing information. If you are just evaluating for 90 days, this is unnecessary.

    Figure 40.    VCF successful deployment

Volume and VMFS datastore

  • After you install the SDC on each host, create a volume through PowerFlex Manager and map that volume to each of the hosts. This volume will serve as the VMFS datastore for the workload domain deployment.

    Step 1

    Begin by navigating in PowerFlex Manager to Block -> Volumes. Click Create Volume in the left-hand corner, enter in the required information, and click Create in Figure 43.

    Figure 43.    Step 1 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 2

    When the grey pop-up box appears after volume creation in Figure 15, click Map. If the box disappears too quickly, simply check the box next to the new volume and navigate to Provision -> Map. In the mapping screen below, use the check boxes to select each new ESXi management node and click Map.

    Figure 44.    Step 2 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 3

    You must create a new VMFS datastore on the volume after you map it to the workload hosts. Log in to the new vCenter, right-click on the cluster and select Storage -> New Datastore to start the datastore wizard.

    Figure 45.    Step 3 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 4

    Begin by selecting the datastore type. In this deployment we use VMFS. Click NEXT.

    Figure 46.    Step 4 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 5

    Enter a Datastore name that identifies its purpose. In this implementation the name is WKLD_DOMAIN. Next select one of the ESXi hosts from the drop-down list. As we mapped the volume to all the workload hosts, any one will work. You will see a list of available volumes, among which will be the 4 TB (in this example) PowerFlex volume. Use the radio button to highlight it and click NEXT.

    Figure 47.    Step 5 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 6

    When you choose VMFS as the type you must choose with which version to format the volume. Dell recommends using the default VMFS 6. Click NEXT after choosing.

    Figure 48.    Step 6 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 7

    In the Partition configuration screen do not change the defaults and click NEXT to review.

    Figure 49.    Step 7 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Step 8

    In the last step, review and then click FINISH to create the datastore.

    Figure 50.    Step 8 – Volume and VMFS datastore

    Once the datastore appears in the list of available datastores in Figure 23, be sure that each ESXi recognizes the new datastore before proceeding. This may require running a Rescan Storage… seen in Figure 45.

    Figure 51.    WKLD_DOMAIN datastore

    Note: After creating the datastore for the workload domain, Dell strongly recommends using Storage vMotion to relocate the vCenter VM to the new datastore. There is a known Broadcom issue in which the VMs the installer creates will deploy to the datastore where the vCenter resides, even if it is local. If the datastore is small, the installer will fail.

    Final task

    Complete the final task below for vSphere HA and DRS. Be sure to create two new heartbeat datastores for the workload domain. Do not map the management domain heartbeat datastores to the workload domain servers.

    1. Heartbeat for vSphere HA

    Because the deployment of the workload domain is brownfield, there is no requirement for a vMotion pool nor to commission hosts. The wizard will ingest the new vCenter and deploy any additional components like NSX Manager.

    Workload wizard

    After completing the prerequisites, initiate the workload wizard by navigating in VCF Operations to Inventory -> VCF Instances -> <instance name>. After highlighting the instance, the ADD WORKLOAD DOMAIN menu appears in the right-hand panel. Use the drop-down box in Figure 52 and select Import a vCenter for the brownfield implementation.

    Figure 52.    Add workload domain: Import a vCenter

    This will initiate the wizard. There are a total of seven steps in the workload domain brownfield deployment for VMFS on FC. They follow here.

    Step 1 General Information

    Supply a workload Domain Name in step 1. Click NEXT.

    Figure 53.    Step 1 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 2 vCenter

    Next, enter in the vCenter server FQDN, vCenter Server Root Password, SSO username and SSO user password. If you integrated NSX into the vCenter prior to ingest, then toggle the switch This vCenter is connected to an NSX instance in Figure 54. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 54.    Step 2 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 3 Certificate Thumbprint

    In step 3 you must confirm the thumbprint of the vCenter and acknowledge that you are inherently confirming VCF Operations thumbprints. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 55.    Step 3 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 4 Prechecks

    This next step requires no input as VCF runs prechecks on the vCenter. You must resolve any failures to continue. Click NEXT when all validations succeed with or without acknowledged warnings.

    Figure 56.    Step 4 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 5 Networking

    In Figure 57 choose whether you want to join an existing NSX Manager setup or do a new deployment (default). If you create a new instance, choose a Deployment Size. VMware recommends three nodes, however you must have three ESXi hosts in your workload domain to deploy the high availability model. Here we only have two ESXi hosts and therefore select Single NSX Manager Appliance. Supply the following:

    • Appliance Size
    • Appliance 1 FQDN
    • Appliance Cluster FQDN
    • Administrator Password and confirmation
    • Auditor Password and confirmation

    Finally, as was the case for the management domain, check the box for Configure NSX Overlay using ESXi Management VMkernel Networking to avoid VLAN requirements. Click NEXT to continue.

    Figure 57.    Step 5 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 6 Validate

    The validations in step 6 mirror the prechecks. Once they succeed click NEXT.

    Figure 58.    Step 6 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    Step 7 Review

    The last screen will show all the step information entered. Review carefully and if anything requires changing, you can toggle back to any step and fix it. When ready click FINISH in Figure 59.

    Figure 59.    Step 7 – Deploy VCF workload domain

    You can view the progress of the workload domain creation by navigating to Fleet Management -> Tasks -> VCF Instances -> <instance name> in VCF Operations as shown in Figure 60. The creation of the workload domain does not take as long as the management domain.

    Figure 60.    Tasks – workload domain creation

    When the workload domain creation is complete, you can view it in VCF Operations in Inventory -> VCF Instances -> <workload domain> in Figure 61.

    Figure 61.    PowerFlex-Workload Domain

    The domain is now ready for VM deployment of your chosen workloads.

Workload prerequisites

  • Any node that is part of a VCF deployment requires the user to install ESXi first. This includes the workload domain. Each principal storage type has a minimum number of nodes for the workload domain. For VMFS on FC there must be at least two nodes. VMware recommends using three for enhanced availability, however in this environment there are only two. You prepare the hosts for the workload domain on PowerFlex in the exact same manner as the management domain. The need for two physical networks requires a brownfield implementation which includes installing a vCenter on one of the new hosts and configuring the VDS. Therefore return to the following sections from the management domain installation and complete each of the designated tasks.

    Tasks

    Follow the links below, performing each task in order. Though the sections will reference the management domain, the tasks apply equally to the workload domain.

    1. ESXi installation
    2. vCenter installation
    3. Virtual Distributed Switches (VDS)
    4. SDC installation

    After you install the SDC on each of the workload domain hosts, return here to create the volume and VMFS datastore.
